entries.meaning: The most basic verb in English: it links a subject to what it is, where it is, or what it is like, states that something exists, and does the grammatical work of building continuous tenses and the passive.
examples: She is a pediatrician at the children's hospital.
He was the tallest kid in our class.
It costs nothing to be polite.
They have been good friends since college.
The spare keys are in the drawer by the sink.
I was at the dentist all morning.
Nobody had been in that room for years.
There is a crack in the foundation.
There were four of us in the car.
There have been three outages this month.
The wedding is in June.
The fire was two years ago this week.
Practice has been on Tuesdays all season.
That will be fourteen fifty.
The total was just under a hundred dollars.
Six times seven is forty-two.
She is working late tonight.
We were driving home when the hail started.
He has been studying since noon.
The road was repaved last summer.
Ballots are counted by hand in this county.
The house has been sold twice since we moved out.
Have you ever been to New Orleans?
I have been to that museum twice.
By the time she was ten she had been to nine states.
The president is to speak at noon.
We were to meet at six, but she never showed.
No one is to leave before the inspector gets here.
You are being ridiculous.
The kids were being unusually quiet.
I know I am being difficult about the date.

senses.head: Link a subject to a description
body: The core copula use: the subject equals, or is described by, what follows. In American speech the present forms almost always contract — I'm, he's, they're — and Russian normally drops the verb entirely in the present. (быть, являться)
examples: She is a pediatrician at the children's hospital.
He was the tallest kid in our class.
It costs nothing to be polite.
They have been good friends since college.

senses.head: Be somewhere, be present
body: Location or attendance rather than identity. This is the sense behind Is anybody home? and Where were you? (находиться, быть (где-л.))
examples: The spare keys are in the drawer by the sink.
I was at the dentist all morning.
Nobody had been in that room for years.

senses.head: Exist; there is / there are
body: The existential pattern uses a dummy there, and the verb agrees with the noun that follows it: there is a problem, there are problems. (существовать; есть, имеется)
examples: There is a crack in the foundation.
There were four of us in the car.
There have been three outages this month.

senses.head: Happen, take place
body: Used of events with a time or a place attached, where it stands in for take place. (быть, состояться, происходить)
examples: The wedding is in June.
The fire was two years ago this week.
Practice has been on Tuesdays all season.

senses.head: Cost, come to, equal
body: Prices at the register and arithmetic on the page. A cashier says that'll be; math says six times seven is forty-two. (стоить; равняться)
examples: That will be fourteen fifty.
The total was just under a hundred dollars.
Six times seven is forty-two.

senses.head: Auxiliary: continuous tenses
body: Be + -ing builds every progressive tense; the auxiliary carries the tense so the main verb does not have to. (вспомогательный глагол (Continuous))
examples: She is working late tonight.
We were driving home when the hail started.
He has been studying since noon.

senses.head: Auxiliary: the passive
body: Be + past participle turns the object of an action into the subject of the sentence. Any tense of be can do it. (вспомогательный глагол (страдательный залог))
examples: The road was repaved last summer.
Ballots are counted by hand in this county.
The house has been sold twice since we moved out.

senses.head: have been to — visited and come back
body: Been fills in for gone when the trip is over: She has been to Denver means she went and returned, while She has gone to Denver means she is still away. (побывать (где-л.))
examples: Have you ever been to New Orleans?
I have been to that museum twice.
By the time she was ten she had been to nine states.

senses.head: be to + verb — scheduled or required
body: Formal, common in news writing and in instructions: an arrangement, an order, or something due to happen. In the past it usually hints that the plan fell through. (должен, предстоит)
examples: The president is to speak at noon.
We were to meet at six, but she never showed.
No one is to leave before the inspector gets here.

senses.head: be being — acting that way for now
body: The progressive of the copula, limited to behavior and temporary states: He is being rude describes this moment, while He has been rude reports what happened. (вести себя (в данный момент))
examples: You are being ridiculous.
The kids were being unusually quiet.
I know I am being difficult about the date.

entries.register: everyday — the most-used verb in the language; no American gets through a sentence without it
entries.contrast: Be has two past forms — was after I / he / she / it, were after you / we / they — so ✗ We was late. The participle needs a helping verb: ✗ I been there twice, but I have been there twice. Keep been apart from being: He has been rude reports something that happened, He is being rude describes him right now. In American speech been usually rhymes with bin, not with bean.
entries.verb type: linking (copular) in the core senses — identity, location, existence, occurrence, price (she is a pediatrician, the total was a hundred dollars) — and auxiliary in senses 6–7, building every progressive (she is working) and every passive (the road was repaved). Stative except the behavior progressive he is being rude.
entries.transitivity: intransitive — be never takes an object, only a subject complement, and that complement is obligatory: the keys are in the drawer, but ✗ She is. outside the existential There is.
entries.passive: no — be builds everyone else's passive and has none of its own: ✗ A pediatrician is been by her. Copulas and auxiliaries do not passivize.
entries.phrasal verbs: be after · be along · be around · be down · be down with · be in · be in for · be in on · be into · be off · be on · be on to · be out · be out of · be over · be through · be up · be up for · be up to

entries.meaning: Hit something over and over, defeat an opponent, or move in a steady rhythm.
examples: A team that sloppy can still beat us.
We beat Chicago 4-1 last October.
Our rowing club has beaten every school in the state this season.
He beat the rug with a broom handle until the dust stopped coming.
She beats the drum on the downbeat.
The prisoners had been beaten before anyone reached them.
Rain beat against the windows all night.
The surf beats on those rocks year-round.
The sun had beaten down on the roof all afternoon.
I could feel my heart beat against my ribs.
His pulse beat faster than the monitor liked.
Her heart has beaten on that pacemaker for nine years.
She beats two eggs into the batter first.
Beat the cream until it holds a peak.
I beat the frosting by hand and regretted it.
A cold sandwich beats nothing at all.
It beat sitting in traffic for two hours.
You can't beat their prices on lumber.
We left at four to beat the traffic.
She beat me to the last parking spot.
They had beaten the storm home by twenty minutes.
Two guys beat him up outside the bar.
Don't beat yourself up over one bad quarter.
He looked like he had been beaten up.
I am beat — I'm going to bed.
We were all beat after the drive from Denver.
By Sunday night the whole crew was beat.

senses.head: Defeat, win against
body: Games, elections, and rivals of any kind. Edited American English keeps the -en after have — we have beaten them — though casual sports talk often says have beat. (побеждать, обыгрывать)
examples: A team that sloppy can still beat us.
We beat Chicago 4-1 last October.
Our rowing club has beaten every school in the state this season.

senses.head: Hit repeatedly
body: Repeated blows with a fist, a stick, or a drumstick. A single blow is hit or strike; beat implies more than one. (бить, колотить)
examples: He beat the rug with a broom handle until the dust stopped coming.
She beats the drum on the downbeat.
The prisoners had been beaten before anyone reached them.

senses.head: Strike against something over and over
body: Intransitive, of rain, waves, wind, or sun, usually with against, on, or down on. (хлестать, стучать, биться (обо что-л.))
examples: Rain beat against the windows all night.
The surf beats on those rocks year-round.
The sun had beaten down on the roof all afternoon.

senses.head: Throb, pulse
body: Of the heart or the pulse, and by extension of wings — the hawk beat its wings twice. (биться (о сердце), пульсировать)
examples: I could feel my heart beat against my ribs.
His pulse beat faster than the monitor liked.
Her heart has beaten on that pacemaker for nine years.

senses.head: Mix or whisk (cooking)
body: Kitchen sense: stir hard and fast with a fork, a whisk, or a mixer. (взбивать (яйца, тесто, сливки))
examples: She beats two eggs into the batter first.
Beat the cream until it holds a peak.
I beat the frosting by hand and regretted it.

senses.head: Be better than (informal)
body: Informal, usually in the frame it beats or you can't beat, followed by a noun or an -ing form. (лучше, чем)
examples: A cold sandwich beats nothing at all.
It beat sitting in traffic for two hours.
You can't beat their prices on lumber.

senses.head: Get there first, beat a deadline
body: Arrive or act before someone or something else: beat the traffic, beat the rain, beat someone to it. (опередить, успеть раньше)
examples: We left at four to beat the traffic.
She beat me to the last parking spot.
They had beaten the storm home by twenty minutes.

senses.head: beat up — attack and injure
body: Separable — beat him up, not beat up him. Reflexively, beat yourself up means to keep blaming yourself for something. (избить)
examples: Two guys beat him up outside the bar.
Don't beat yourself up over one bad quarter.
He looked like he had been beaten up.

senses.head: be beat — worn out
body: Informal and adjectival, and the one place where the short form is standard: I'm beat for tiredness, never I'm beaten. (измотан, без сил)
examples: I am beat — I'm going to bed.
We were all beat after the drive from Denver.
By Sunday night the whole crew was beat.

entries.register: everyday — one of the verbs an American uses without thinking, in sports talk, the kitchen, and plain speech
entries.contrast: The past is spelled and said exactly like the base — ✗ beated — so only the participle marks the group: beaten. Edited American English keeps that -en: We have beaten them twice, not We have beat them twice, though the shorter form is common in casual sports talk. Beat also survives as an adjective meaning worn out: I'm beat.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic in every documented sense: defeat, strike repeatedly, throb, whisk, outrun a deadline. The I'm beat of sense 9 is an adjective, not a verb form.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive in the defeat, hitting, cooking, and get-there-first senses (we beat Chicago 4-1, beat the cream, she beat me to the spot), intransitive of rain, surf, and hearts (rain beat against the windows, my pulse beat faster).
entries.passive: yes in the transitive senses — the prisoners had been beaten before anyone reached them, he looked like he had been beaten up. No passive of the intransitive the surf beats on those rocks.
entries.phrasal verbs: beat back · beat down · beat off · beat out · beat up · beat up on

entries.meaning: Bully someone into doing something by badgering, hectoring, or intimidating them.
examples: Don't let them browbeat you into signing anything today.
She browbeats her little brother into doing her chores.
The attorney browbeat the witness until the judge stepped in.
Management has browbeaten the staff about the new schedule for weeks.
Everyone left the meeting feeling browbeaten.
He had the browbeaten look of a man who never wins an argument.
Two suppliers had been browbeaten into cutting their prices.

senses.head: Bully into doing something
body: Pressure applied with words rather than force, usually in the frame browbeat someone into doing something. It follows beat form for form, so the past looks like the base. (запугивать, принуждать (давлением))
examples: Don't let them browbeat you into signing anything today.
She browbeats her little brother into doing her chores.
The attorney browbeat the witness until the judge stepped in.
Management has browbeaten the staff about the new schedule for weeks.

senses.head: browbeaten — cowed, worn down
body: The participle used as an adjective or in the passive, describing someone left meek by constant pressure. (запуганный, забитый)
examples: Everyone left the meeting feeling browbeaten.
He had the browbeaten look of a man who never wins an argument.
Two suppliers had been browbeaten into cutting their prices.

entries.register: rare — a prefixed derivative of beat that Americans recognize but seldom produce; everyday speech says bully or pressure
entries.contrast: It follows beat form for form, so the past looks like the base — ✗ browbeated — and the participle takes -en. Note the stress: browbeat keeps it on the first part, unlike the go compounds in this group, which stress the second.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic, a verb of verbal pressure. The participle browbeaten doubles as an adjective: he had the browbeaten look of a man who never wins an argument.
entries.transitivity: transitive only, with an obligatory human object, typically in the frame browbeat someone into doing something: the attorney browbeat the witness; ✗ The attorney browbeat until the judge stepped in.
entries.passive: yes, and it is common — two suppliers had been browbeaten into cutting their prices; everyone left the meeting feeling browbeaten.

entries.meaning: Cut a shape out of a hard material, slice cooked meat, or cut a piece out of something larger.
examples: Every October he carves a pumpkin for the porch.
My grandfather taught me how to carve birds out of pine.
A neighbor has carved a bench out of the fallen oak.
Who carves the roast at your house?
He carved the ham into slices too thick for sandwiches.
By the time we sat down, my uncle had carved the turkey.
She carved her initials into the picnic table.
Please don't carve anything into that bench.
Somebody had carved a date into the beam above the door.
She carved out a niche selling used farm equipment online.
We carved out two hours on Friday for the review.
He has carved out a reputation as the guy who answers the phone.
Developers carved up the old dairy farm into forty lots.
Three chains have carved up the whole grocery market here.
The museum keeps a carven panel from an old Norwegian church.
Rows of carven saints line the choir stalls.

senses.head: Cut a shape from wood or stone
body: The core sense: shape a hard material by cutting away at it. In modern American English the verb is fully regular — carve, carved, carved. (вырезать, высекать (из дерева, камня, кости))
examples: Every October he carves a pumpkin for the porch.
My grandfather taught me how to carve birds out of pine.
A neighbor has carved a bench out of the fallen oak.

senses.head: Slice cooked meat
body: The table sense, most often heard about a turkey or a roast at a holiday dinner. (разрезать, нарезать (мясо))
examples: Who carves the roast at your house?
He carved the ham into slices too thick for sandwiches.
By the time we sat down, my uncle had carved the turkey.

senses.head: Cut letters or marks into a surface
body: Incising rather than shaping: initials in a tree, a date in a beam, a name in stone. (вырезать (надпись), высекать)
examples: She carved her initials into the picnic table.
Please don't carve anything into that bench.
Somebody had carved a date into the beam above the door.

senses.head: carve out — make a place by effort
body: Figurative: take something out of a larger whole through effort — a niche, a career, an hour in a full day. (выкроить, создать (нишу, время, репутацию))
examples: She carved out a niche selling used farm equipment online.
We carved out two hours on Friday for the review.
He has carved out a reputation as the guy who answers the phone.

senses.head: carve up — divide into pieces
body: Usually disapproving, of land, markets, or an estate split among competing claimants. (делить, дробить (на части))
examples: Developers carved up the old dairy farm into forty lots.
Three chains have carved up the whole grocery market here.

senses.head: carven — literary adjective
body: An old participle that survives only as a literary adjective in front of a noun — a carven door, carven stone — and never after have. (резной)
examples: The museum keeps a carven panel from an old Norwegian church.
Rows of carven saints line the choir stalls.

entries.forms: carve /kɑrv/ · carved /kɑrvd/ · carved /kɑrvd/ — archaic participle carven /ˈkɑrvən/; the past corve that the source list records is not an English word
entries.register: everyday — carving a pumpkin or a turkey is ordinary American talk; only the leftover participle carven is literary
entries.third person: carves · -ing form: carving (the silent e drops)
entries.contrast: In modern American English carve is an ordinary regular verb: carve — carved — carved. It belongs to this group only because of carven, an old participle that now survives just as a literary adjective — a carven door, carven stone — and never after have: ✗ I have carven the turkey. The past corve that appears in some Russian tables is not an English word at all; use carved. Compare grave and shave, which kept graven and shaven the same way.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic throughout: shaping wood or stone, slicing meat, incising letters, and the figurative carve out / carve up. Carven is no longer a verb form, only a literary adjective — ✗ I have carven the turkey.
entries.transitivity: both, but overwhelmingly transitive (carve a pumpkin, carve her initials into the table, carve out two hours); the object drops only in the absolute use Who carves at your house?
entries.passive: yes — the turkey had been carved by the time we sat down, the old dairy farm was carved up into forty lots.

entries.meaning: Come or go before something else in time or order — a formal verb now met mostly as the foregoing and a foregone conclusion.
examples: In the older service, a hymn would forego the sermon.
Months of quiet rehearsal forewent opening night.
The events that have foregone the treaty are covered in chapter two.
Two smaller quakes had foregone the big one by about a week.
The foregoing section explains where the numbers come from.
Nothing in the foregoing limits your right to cancel.
His reelection was a foregone conclusion by the third quarter.
The verdict felt like a foregone conclusion before the trial even started.
The board voted to forego raises this year — an editor would make that forgo.
You will see forego the fee on plenty of websites, though forgo is the standard spelling.

senses.head: Come or go before
body: The literal sense — fore- plus go. Formal and rare in its finite forms today; you will meet it mostly in older, legal, or academic prose. (предшествовать)
examples: In the older service, a hymn would forego the sermon.
Months of quiet rehearsal forewent opening night.
The events that have foregone the treaty are covered in chapter two.
Two smaller quakes had foregone the big one by about a week.

senses.head: the foregoing — what was said above
body: Legal and academic writing, used as an adjective or as a noun: the foregoing paragraph, nothing in the foregoing. (вышеизложенное, вышесказанное)
examples: The foregoing section explains where the numbers come from.
Nothing in the foregoing limits your right to cancel.

senses.head: a foregone conclusion — settled in advance
body: A fixed phrase, and the most common place the participle still turns up. Keep the e: foregone conclusion, not forgone. (предрешённый исход)
examples: His reelection was a foregone conclusion by the third quarter.
The verdict felt like a foregone conclusion before the trial even started.

senses.head: Spelling variant of forgo
body: Dictionaries do record forego for forgo (do without), and it appears in print, but careful American editing keeps the two words apart. (= forgo: отказываться, воздерживаться (от чего-л.))
examples: The board voted to forego raises this year — an editor would make that forgo.
You will see forego the fee on plenty of websites, though forgo is the standard spelling.

entries.register: rare — the "go before" verb is dead in ordinary use; Americans meet it only as the foregoing and a foregone conclusion
entries.third person: foregoes (-es after the o) · -ing form: foregoing
entries.contrast: Forego and forgo sound identical but do opposite work: forego means "go before," forgo means "do without." The finite forms of forego are formal and rare today; what you actually meet is foregoing ("the foregoing paragraph") and foregone in the fixed phrase a foregone conclusion. Dictionaries do record forego as a variant spelling of forgo, but careful American editing keeps the two words apart.
entries.verb type: action in the literal 'come or go before' sense, though the subject is an event rather than an agent (months of quiet rehearsal forewent opening night). What survives in live American English is adjectival: the foregoing section, a foregone conclusion.
entries.transitivity: transitive — the object is what the subject precedes: a hymn would forego the sermon. No intransitive use; the finite forms are formal and rare either way.
entries.passive: restricted — formally possible but effectively unattested (the sermon was foregone by a hymn reads as an error for forgone); the participle lives on only as the adjective in a foregone conclusion.

entries.meaning: Choose to do without something you could have had, or give up a claim to it.
examples: I'll forgo dessert tonight.
Plenty of owners forgo a salary in the first year.
She forwent the bonus so her team could split it.
He has forgone two vacations to finish the house.
The lender agreed to forgo interest for six months.
The heirs forwent any claim on the house.
They had forgone health coverage for years before the new plan.
The tax break cost the state about ninety million in forgone revenue.
Their estimate includes forgone wages for the months she was out of work.

senses.head: Do without, go without
body: The everyday sense: give up something available to you, usually by choice. The past forwent is correct but rare — most Americans say went without or gave up. (отказаться, обойтись без (чего-л.))
examples: I'll forgo dessert tonight.
Plenty of owners forgo a salary in the first year.
She forwent the bonus so her team could split it.
He has forgone two vacations to finish the house.

senses.head: Waive a right or a payment
body: Formal, legal, and financial: a party forgoes interest, fees, or a claim it could otherwise enforce. (отказаться от (права, выплаты))
examples: The lender agreed to forgo interest for six months.
The heirs forwent any claim on the house.
They had forgone health coverage for years before the new plan.

senses.head: forgone income — money not earned
body: Economics and accounting: forgone revenue, forgone wages — the cost of a choice measured by what it gave up. (недополученный доход, упущенная выгода)
examples: The tax break cost the state about ninety million in forgone revenue.
Their estimate includes forgone wages for the months she was out of work.

entries.register: neutral to formal — ordinary in writing, especially legal and financial prose; speech says give up or do without, and the past forwent is rare anywhere
entries.third person: forgoes (-es after the o) · -ing form: forgoing
entries.contrast: Same sound as forego, different job: forgo is the one that means "do without" — forgo dessert, forgo a salary. The past forwent is correct but rare; in ordinary American writing gave up or did without usually takes its place. And forgone is not the foregone of a foregone conclusion, which keeps the e.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic, a deliberate choice to do without. Forgone also serves as an adjective in the economics sense: forgone revenue, forgone wages.
entries.transitivity: transitive, object obligatory — I'll forgo dessert, the lender agreed to forgo interest for six months; ✗ The lender agreed to forgo.
entries.passive: restricted — grammatical but stiff and rare (the bonus was forgone so the team could split it); American writing keeps it active or reaches for the adjective, ninety million in forgone revenue.

entries.meaning: Move or travel from one place to another, leave, or — in dozens of extended uses — become, turn out, run, fit, fail, or stop.
examples: We go to my sister's every Thanksgiving.
They went to the coast for three days.
My roommate has gone to the store.
It's late — I should go.
She went without saying goodbye.
Everyone had gone home by nine o'clock.
The milk went sour in one hot afternoon.
If the power fails, the alarms go dead.
Three of the mills have gone bankrupt since spring.
How did the interview go?
The first day went better than I expected.
Rehearsals have gone smoothly so far.
This road goes all the way to the lake.
The old fence went right through where the barn is now.
The trail has gone around that ridge ever since they rerouted it.
The big pot goes in the cabinet under the sink.
Those files went in the gray box.
That couch will never go through this doorway.
The transmission went at a hundred and ten thousand miles.
His hearing is going in one ear.
Half the paycheck had gone to rent before he ever saw it.
The cookies are all gone.
I am going to call her tonight.
It is going to rain before we finish.
We were going to drive, but the flights got cheap.
He goes running before work.
We went fishing on Saturday.
I have never gone skiing.
That shirt does not go with those pants.
The blue rug went better with the couch than the green one.
Six goes into forty-eight eight times.
The argument went on for an hour.
What is going on out there?
The strike has gone on longer than either side planned.
The smoke alarm goes off every time I use the broiler.
The flash went off right in my eyes.
Two alarms had gone off before anybody called it in.
The lights went out across three counties.
We hardly ever go out on weeknights.
Her parents had gone out for the evening.
She went through a rough divorce last year.
Go through the file and pull anything from 2019.
Customs had gone through every bag on the flight.

senses.head: Move or travel to a place
body: The core sense, away from the speaker. Note the gone / been split: She has gone to Denver means she is still away, while She has been to Denver means she went and came back. (идти, ехать, ходить)
examples: We go to my sister's every Thanksgiving.
They went to the coast for three days.
My roommate has gone to the store.

senses.head: Leave, depart
body: Intransitive, with no destination named. I have to go means either leaving or, politely, using the bathroom. (уходить, уезжать)
examples: It's late — I should go.
She went without saying goodbye.
Everyone had gone home by nine o'clock.

senses.head: Become (usually a worse state)
body: A linking use with an adjective: go bad, go blind, go bankrupt, go gray, go crazy. Nearly always a change for the worse — improvements take get or turn. (становиться, делаться)
examples: The milk went sour in one hot afternoon.
If the power fails, the alarms go dead.
Three of the mills have gone bankrupt since spring.

senses.head: Turn out, proceed
body: How an event or a process works out — the sense behind How did it go? and the meeting went well. (проходить, идти (об успехе дела))
examples: How did the interview go?
The first day went better than I expected.
Rehearsals have gone smoothly so far.

senses.head: Lead, extend, run
body: Of roads, fences, wires, or ranges: the subject does not move, it stretches from one place to another. (вести, идти, тянуться)
examples: This road goes all the way to the lake.
The old fence went right through where the barn is now.
The trail has gone around that ridge ever since they rerouted it.

senses.head: Belong, have its place
body: Where a thing is kept or whether it fits: Where do the plates go?, It won't go through the door. (быть на месте, класться, помещаться)
examples: The big pot goes in the cabinet under the sink.
Those files went in the gray box.
That couch will never go through this doorway.

senses.head: Give out, run out, be used up
body: Of things that fail or disappear — a transmission, someone's hearing, the last of the coffee. The participle is common as a bare adjective: the money is gone. (кончаться; отказывать, ломаться)
examples: The transmission went at a hundred and ten thousand miles.
His hearing is going in one ear.
Half the paycheck had gone to rent before he ever saw it.
The cookies are all gone.

senses.head: be going to — future or intention
body: The ordinary spoken future, for plans already made and for predictions with visible evidence. In speech it reduces to gonna. (собираться (что-л. сделать))
examples: I am going to call her tonight.
It is going to rain before we finish.
We were going to drive, but the flights got cheap.

senses.head: go + -ing — do an activity
body: A fixed pattern for sports and errands: go fishing, go running, go shopping. Watch the preposition — you go swimming in the lake, not to the lake. (ходить (плавать, за покупками и т. п.))
examples: He goes running before work.
We went fishing on Saturday.
I have never gone skiing.

senses.head: Match, suit, fit with
body: Of colors, flavors, or furniture, usually as go with. The same verb covers arithmetic: three goes into twelve four times. (подходить, сочетаться)
examples: That shirt does not go with those pants.
The blue rug went better with the couch than the green one.
Six goes into forty-eight eight times.

senses.head: go on — continue; happen
body: Two everyday uses: keep doing something, and — with what — be taking place. On its own, Go on! means keep talking. (продолжаться; происходить)
examples: The argument went on for an hour.
What is going on out there?
The strike has gone on longer than either side planned.

senses.head: go off — explode, sound; spoil
body: Of bombs, guns, and alarms; also of food turning bad, though Americans usually say go bad for that. Go off on someone means lose your temper at them. (сработать, взорваться; испортиться)
examples: The smoke alarm goes off every time I use the broiler.
The flash went off right in my eyes.
Two alarms had gone off before anybody called it in.

senses.head: go out — be extinguished; go out socially
body: A fire or a light goes out; people go out for the evening, and go out with someone means date them. (погаснуть; выходить (в свет), встречаться)
examples: The lights went out across three counties.
We hardly ever go out on weeknights.
Her parents had gone out for the evening.

senses.head: go through — endure; search
body: Live through something hard, or look through things one by one. Go through with means carry out a plan you were hesitant about. (пережить; просмотреть, перебрать)
examples: She went through a rough divorce last year.
Go through the file and pull anything from 2019.
Customs had gone through every bag on the flight.

entries.register: everyday — one of the verbs an American uses without thinking
entries.third person: goes (-es after the o) · -ing form: going
entries.contrast: Went is the past and stands on its own; gone is the participle and needs have, has, or had. ✗ I have went to the bank and ✗ He gone home already are the two classic errors — say I went to the bank and He has gone home already. There is also a gone / been split: She has gone to Denver means she is still away, while She has been to Denver means she went and came back.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic in the movement, departure, process, and give-out senses (they went to the coast, the transmission went). Also linking (copular) with a bare adjective in go bad, go sour, go blind, go bankrupt — almost always a change for the worse.
entries.transitivity: intransitive in every sense the entry documents; destinations, paths, and complements arrive through prepositions or particles (go to the store, go through the file, go with those pants). Even six goes into forty-eight is intransitive.
entries.passive: no — with no object there is nothing to promote: ✗ The coast was gone to by them, ✗ Home had been gone by everyone. Only the prepositional phrasal go through allows a marginal passive in casual speech — every bag had been gone through.
entries.phrasal verbs: go about · go after · go against · go ahead · go along · go along with · go around · go at · go away · go back · go back on · go by · go down · go down on · go for · go in for · go into · go off · go off on · go on · go out · go over · go through · go through with · go under · go up · go with · go without

entries.meaning: Cut the wool or hair off an animal, or cut and snap cleanly through something.
examples: They shear the flock every spring.
The crew sheared four hundred ewes on Saturday.
Every animal on the place has been shorn.
By noon the ranch had shorn half the herd.
The recruits were shorn the first morning.
A barber sheared his curls off in about a minute.
She has been shorn nearly to the scalp for the treatments.
A rivet can shear long before it pulls out.
The bolt sheared off under the load.
Ice has sheared those pilings clean off twice.
The company came out of the lawsuit shorn of its patents.
By 1919 the emperor had been shorn of every real power.

senses.head: Shear a sheep, cut off wool
body: The primary sense, and the one that takes shorn: a shorn sheep, the flock has been shorn. The past is sheared. (стричь (овец))
examples: They shear the flock every spring.
The crew sheared four hundred ewes on Saturday.
Every animal on the place has been shorn.
By noon the ranch had shorn half the herd.

senses.head: Crop hair close
body: Of people, and usually severe or forced — recruits, prisoners, patients. Most often passive with shorn. (остричь, обрить)
examples: The recruits were shorn the first morning.
A barber sheared his curls off in about a minute.
She has been shorn nearly to the scalp for the treatments.

senses.head: Snap or cut cleanly through (mechanics)
body: Engineering sense: metal failing under a sideways load. Here the participle is sheared, never shorn — the bolt sheared off. (срезать(ся), ломаться (о болте, металле))
examples: A rivet can shear long before it pulls out.
The bolt sheared off under the load.
Ice has sheared those pilings clean off twice.

senses.head: shorn of — stripped of
body: Figurative and formal, passive only: left without power, rights, or assets. (лишённый (чего-л.))
examples: The company came out of the lawsuit shorn of its patents.
By 1919 the emperor had been shorn of every real power.

entries.forms: shear /ʃɪr/ · sheared /ʃɪrd/ (the source list records the archaic shore /ʃɔr/) · shorn /ʃɔrn/ (also sheared /ʃɪrd/)
entries.register: rare — specialized: sheep and wool on one side, engineering on the other; ordinary Americans say cut or clip
entries.contrast: Both participles are current in American English, and they split by sense: shorn for wool, hair, and anything figuratively stripped away — shorn sheep, shorn of authority — and sheared for machinery and for metal that snaps under load: the bolt sheared off. The past is sheared; the shore listed in older tables is archaic and today reads as the noun shore. Do not confuse the verb with its homophone, the adjective sheer /ʃɪr/.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic. The participle splits by sense: shorn for wool, hair, and figurative stripping (shorn of authority), sheared for metal snapping under load (the bolt sheared off).
entries.transitivity: both — transitive of animals and hair (they shear the flock every spring, a barber sheared his curls off), intransitive in the mechanical sense (a rivet can shear long before it pulls out).
entries.passive: yes in the transitive senses, and often the preferred form — every animal on the place has been shorn, the recruits were shorn the first morning. Shorn of is passive-only: by 1919 the emperor had been shorn of every real power. No passive of the intransitive the bolt sheared off.

entries.meaning: Experience something done to you — a process, a treatment, a change — or endure something difficult.
examples: All new hires undergo two weeks of training.
She underwent knee surgery in March.
By the time it shipped, the design had undergone six revisions.
Steel undergoes stress you can't see.
The language underwent a major shift in that century.
The neighborhood has undergone a lot of change since 2010.
No family should have to undergo that twice.
Prisoners underwent months of interrogation.
The crew had undergone worse on the previous crossing.

senses.head: Go through a process or treatment
body: Almost always transitive, with an event or procedure as the object: surgery, training, testing, review. It never describes physical travel, unlike go. (проходить, подвергаться (процедуре, обучению))
examples: All new hires undergo two weeks of training.
She underwent knee surgery in March.
By the time it shipped, the design had undergone six revisions.

senses.head: Experience a change
body: Of places, materials, and institutions changing over time; the subject is affected rather than acting. (претерпевать (изменения))
examples: Steel undergoes stress you can't see.
The language underwent a major shift in that century.
The neighborhood has undergone a lot of change since 2010.

senses.head: Endure something difficult
body: Formal, of hardship borne rather than chosen: undergo hardship, undergo an ordeal. (переносить, испытывать (трудности))
examples: No family should have to undergo that twice.
Prisoners underwent months of interrogation.
The crew had undergone worse on the previous crossing.

entries.register: neutral to formal — ordinary in writing, especially medical and news prose; speech says have or go through
entries.third person: undergoes (-es after the o) · -ing form: undergoing
entries.contrast: It inherits every form from go, so ✗ undergoed and ✗ has underwent. Unlike go, it is almost always transitive and takes an event or process as its object — you undergo surgery, testing, a change — and it never describes physical travel.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic but non-agentive: the subject is the one something is done to (the design had undergone six revisions, she underwent knee surgery). No linking or stative use, and it never means physical travel the way go does.
entries.transitivity: transitive, object obligatory, and the object is always a process, treatment, or change: undergo two weeks of training, undergo an ordeal; ✗ All new hires undergo.
entries.passive: no — the subject is already the affected party, so promotion has nowhere to go: ✗ Knee surgery was undergone by her, ✗ Six revisions had been undergone by the design. Keep it active, or say she had knee surgery.
